young.html: In 1787 the new Constitution had been written, but it would only take effect if the states agreed. In New York many people opposed it. So three men, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison and John Jay, wrote 85 newspaper essays explaining why it was a good plan. They signed them all with one made-up name: Publius.

One big idea was about groups, which Madison called factions. People will always form groups that want different things. In a small country, one big group could gang up on everyone else. In a large country with many groups, it's harder for any one group to take over.

Another big idea: the government should be split into parts that can check each other. Madison wrote, "If men were angels, no government would be necessary." Since we're not angels, power must be watched.

young.name: gb-factions
young.cap: Make the republic bigger and see how many different interests there are. Can any one group win a majority alone?

young.html: Write to the newspaper. Pick a family or school rule you think is good. Write a short letter explaining why, as if for a newspaper, and sign it with a pen name like Publius. Read it aloud. Did your reasons convince anyone?

full.html: The Federalist appeared in New York newspapers from October 1787 to 1788 and was collected in two volumes in 1788. Hamilton planned it and wrote the most essays (51 by the common count), Madison wrote 29 and Jay, who fell ill, 5; the authorship of a dozen essays was long disputed, and most scholars now credit them to Madison. The Teddy Rook Book's Federalist Papers guide has all 85 essays with notes.

Madison defines a faction as a group, majority or minority, moved by a passion or interest against the rights of others or the good of the whole. Its causes are "sown in the nature of man," above all in the unequal distribution of property. We can't remove the causes without destroying liberty, so we must control the effects. A pure democracy can't do this, but a large republic can:

full.text: Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens; or if such a common motive exists, it will be more difficult for all who feel it to discover their own strength, and to act in unison with each other.
full.author: Publius (Hamilton, Madison and Jay)

full.name: gb-factions
full.cap: Madison's argument as a picture: the more interests a republic contains, the smaller the largest one is likely to be.

full.html: Separation of powers, Madison says, needs more than words on paper. Each branch must have the means and motive to resist the others: "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition."

full.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary. If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary. In framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.
full.author: Publius (Hamilton, Madison and Jay)

items: No. 1 (Hamilton): whether societies can establish good government "from reflection and choice" or must depend on "accident and force."
Nos. 2–5 (Jay): the need for union for safety against foreign powers.
Nos. 15–22: the defects of the Articles of Confederation.
No. 39 (Madison): the new government is partly national, partly federal.
No. 47 (Madison): Montesquieu and the separation of powers.
No. 78 (Hamilton): the judiciary as "the least dangerous" branch and the courts' power to declare laws void that conflict with the Constitution.
No. 84 (Hamilton): why he thought a bill of rights unnecessary.

full.html: Publius' method. Each essay takes an objection, states it fairly, and answers it with history, reasoning about human nature and the text of the Constitution.

Thinking The Federalist settled the debate. Anti-Federalist writers such as "Brutus" and "Federal Farmer" answered it point by point, and their worries about a distant government and a missing bill of rights helped bring the Bill of Rights. The Anti-Federalist Papers on this site give their side.

deep.html: Thomas Jefferson called The Federalist the best commentary on the principles of government ever written. American judges and lawyers still cite it to understand what the Constitution's words meant to those who ratified it, though scholars caution that it was a persuasive work written quickly for one state's debate. Hamilton and Madison themselves later disagreed sharply about the meaning of federal powers, for example over a national bank.

Anti-Federalists argued that a large republic would be ruled by a distant elite, that the federal courts and the power to tax would swallow the states, and that liberty needed a written bill of rights. Some historians, notably Charles Beard in 1913, argued that the framers' economic interests shaped the Constitution; later historians found his evidence weak but kept asking whose interests the new government served.
